records.name: Lampung
records.summary:
In November 2018 Satpol PP, the regional moral-and-order force, raided three transwomen in Lampung — an incident a comparative UNSW/Harvard review of violence against transgender women in this country records as police-perpetrated violence. No further incidents, arrests, or enacted local bylaws specific to Lampung were found in the dossier period, and no visitor-facing documents or screening information is recorded.

For a visitor, the practical exposure is a single documented police-contact incident with no campaign evidence: the raid shows that police contact can escalate into documented police-perpetrated violence, but the dossier does not support a patterned risk.

sources.summary: UNSW human-rights review of anti-trans violence in Indonesia: documents that in November 2018 three transwomen were raided by Satpol PP (the regional morals-and-order force) in Lampung province — detained at the Satpol PP office and hosed down at the firefighter building, with an officer recording it — alongside a national pattern of transwomen murdered in 2017 (Bone, Semarang, South Sulawesi) and election-cycle anti-LGBT bylaw lobbying from 2016 onward; an SMRC survey of 1,520 Indonesians (Nov 2016) found LGBT people hated by 16.6%.

OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study analyses discriminatory regional regulations in eight Indonesian provinces — Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera and Yogyakarta — at province and district level; Lampung is named among them, supporting this record's claim of discriminatory regional regulation. records.name: Central Kalimantan
records.summary:
Central Kalimantan shows no sub-national divergence for a visitor: no enacted discriminatory bylaw, raid, arrest or incident series targeting transgender people was found, and the province is not one of the eight identified in OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation analysis of discriminatory regional regulations. Visitor risk therefore tracks the national baseline: the KUHP criminal code in force from 1 January 2026 criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member; because same-sex marriage is not recognised, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction.

Ordinary local moral policing seen in some neighbouring provinces is absent here, but there is no province-specific enforcement record in either direction; any risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence, and a transgender visitor should assume the national criminal baseline applies in full.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa, 2022): mapping of national laws and regional regulations violating rights of women and LGBTIQ people in Indonesia; its eight-province list of discriminatory regional regulations does NOT include Central Kalimantan, which is the basis for treating the earlier 'one of the eight provinces' attribution for this unit as a misplacement of East Kalimantan.

Wikipedia's article on the 2023 Indonesian Penal Code (RUU KUHP) records that the law was passed on 6 December 2022 and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment, and that it criminalises sexual activity outside marriage — unmarried partners face up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The article notes the code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, and that because same-sex marriage is not recognised in Indonesia, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. This is the national criminal baseline a visitor in Central Kalimantan stands under, consistent with this record's finding that the province's risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence.

records.name: North Sumatra
records.summary:
North Sumatra is one of the eight provinces whose regional regulations the national study (OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation) examined as discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, including rules touching sexual orientation and gender expression. No specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted local bylaw targeting transgender people is documented in the dossier, so the signal for a visitor is legal divergence without operational evidence.

Practical reading: the discriminatory-regulations finding is a real but small risk factor absent any enforcement documentation, and the one documented legal-process data point — a local court handling a transgender man's name-change application neutrally over a six-week process, with no enforcement action against the applicant recorded — points to routine if conservative administration rather than active persecution.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

Dimas Cahya, a transgender man from Medan (North Sumatra's capital), described to UNAIDS how he became the first transgender man in Medan to legally change his name to match his identity: after a six-week process the Medan District Court granted the application, and the judge, though warning the change would 'erase my identity', stayed out of LGBTI issues completely. The article frames Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people deemed 'immoral', and reports that a Medan legal-aid organisation asked the couple invasive questions before the case. For this record it is North Sumatra's only documented legal-process data point: a local court handled a trans person's application neutrally and no enforcement action against the couple is recorded anywhere in the article.

records.name: North Sulawesi
records.summary:
North Sulawesi carries no provincial divergence for a visitor: the national study's eight-province list (Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta) does not include it — the Sulawesi entry in the eight is South Sulawesi (the Makassar bylaw province), a different province — and no enforcement incident, raid, arrest, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people was found in the dossier.

A visitor-facing risk profile follows the national picture: the new KUHP code in force January 2026, with police extortion and arbitrary detention the main documented mechanism. One local account documents police harassment of LGBT people during capital-city raids, with no arrests or prosecutions reported in that account.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

On 11 June 2016 LGBT groups joined Manado's women's movement in a street action against sexual violence at Bundaran Zero Point, Manado, from 08.00 to 10.00 WITA; SALUT (Sanubari Sulawesi Utara), the local LGBT organisation whose director Coco Jericho was quoted, took part. The article records that police raids in Manado have included harassment of LGBT people - a butch lesbian groped during a raid, per SALUT - and that victims often do not report because of fear their families will not accept their orientation. It documents a public LGBT+ presence in Manado and a local account of raid-era conduct, with no arrests or prosecutions reported in the piece.

On Saturday 10 November (2012) a waria beach-queen pageant was held at Malalayang beach, Manado, organised by Indonesian parliament member Paula Sinjal together with the National Narcotics Agency of North Sulawesi (BNN) as an outreach event on the dangers of drugs and HIV/AIDS. The report quotes Sinjal saying waria are among local people and deserve attention. It documents official-level engagement with North Sulawesi's waria community through a public pageant - evidence of a visible, organised trans community in Manado - with no adverse official action recorded.

This Konde.co interview profiles Alexa, elected Ratu Waria Sulawesi Utara 2016-2018 at the Sahid Kawanua Hotel in Manado, who says that after her title she suffered discrimination from sensationalist media and the public, with her personal crisis peaking around 25 March 2019. The article confirms a visible trans-women community culture in North Sulawesi - an elected province-level waria queen in Manado - while documenting the media-stoked stigma that follows public visibility. No legal or police action appears anywhere in the account.

records.name: Southeast Sulawesi
records.summary:
Southeast Sulawesi is not among the eight provinces in the national study's analysis of discriminatory regional regulations (the Sulawesi entry in that list is South Sulawesi, a different province), and the dossier records no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted bylaw targeting transgender people; its earlier inclusion in an eight-province bloc was a misattribution. Visitor risk follows the national framework: the KUHP code in force January 2026, with the outside-marriage restriction applying to same-sex couples because same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Community evidence from the provincial capital (a 2024 qualitative study) describes same-sex groups living discreetly — more introverted and careful about expressing feelings after identifying as gay — with no enforcement incident reported in that study; a transgender visitor should expect discretion culture and no documented local enforcement either way.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

A qualitative study by Universitas Halu Oleo researchers, published in Jurnal Budaya Etnika Vol. 8 No. 2 (23 December 2024), describes gay life in Kendari, the capital of Southeast Sulawesi: gay groups in the city say same-sex orientation has partly been converted into an economically valued 'profession', and that after identifying as gay they become more introverted and careful about expressing their feelings to others. The study documents same-sex communities in Kendari living discreetly, with no enforcement incident, raid or local regulation reported in the article. For this record it is the only Southeast Sulawesi-specific community evidence found, and it does not alter the national-framework risk profile described in the record.

records.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
records.summary:
Yogyakarta is among the eight provinces whose regional regulations a national study (OutRight's 'Creeping Criminalisation') examined as discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, yet the dossier documents no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people here: the visitor-facing signal is legal divergence without operational evidence.

The one enforcement-adjacent event documented - the February 2016 closure of the trans-Muslim religious school in this special region after a hardline religious group threatened to seal it - proceeded on administrative and religious grounds rather than under any enacted regional anti-trans regulation, and drew public restraint from the regional government. For a traveller, the practical exposure is a discriminatory regulatory layer whose actual operation against visitors is not documented; no trans-specific incident involving travellers, and no visitor documents or border-screening practice, is recorded in the dossier. sources.summary: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

BBC Indonesia (26 February 2016) reports that on the night of Wednesday 24 February 2016 Yogyakarta's Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah — a religious school where trans women ('waria') study Islam — was closed after the hardline Front Jihad Islam (FJI) threatened to seal it, amid what the BBC describes as rising hate speech against LGBT people 'especially in Yogyakarta'. Banguntapan district head (camat) Jati Bayubroto justified the closure on the grounds the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site; founder Shinta Ratri said about 20 waria attend the weekly weekend classes, which teach ordinary Islamic instruction. The report documents a concrete, Yogyakarta-located enforcement-adjacent event against a trans institution — the first such incident this record's dossier had recorded — while showing the shutdown proceeded on administrative/religious grounds rather than an enacted regional anti-trans regulation.

Rappler Indonesia's 25 February 2016 report details the closure meeting: on 24 February 2016 at about 20:00 WIB a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta — attended by ward/residents' officials, the lurah, the local military district commander and, in the earlier 19 February session, the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief (Kapolsek) — ended with an agreement to shut the Al-Fatah waria pesantren after the Front Jihad Islam demanded it; a waria witness said an FJI leader delivered 'fiery' anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of 'Allahu Akbar' and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, calling LGBT people 'sama-sama anak bangsa' (fellow children of the nation) and saying the regional government would study the issue. It is the first documented Yogyakarta operational-pressure event for this record's dossier, concluded on administrative/community grounds without any provincial anti-trans statute being cited.

DW Indonesia (21 June 2021) reports that Yogyakarta's trans women ('transpuan'/'waria') — most working as street performers or wedding make-up artists and attached to the Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah — saw earnings fall by about 60 percent during the COVID-19 pandemic and were, in DW's words, 'ignored by the government', struggling to pay rent and buy food. The article describes a 12 June 2021 aromatherapy-candle making class at the Al-Fatah pesantren in Yogyakarta run with local small business Malini.yk to teach new income skills, and says the waria kept performing despite donors refusing even masked performances. It shows the Yogyakarta waria community and pesantren operating again years after the 2016 closure, while documenting persistent economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province.
